newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish cabinet agrees on 1998 growth, inflation.
newsitem.headline: Polish cabinet agrees on 1998 growth, inflation.

text.p: Poland's cabinet approved some macroeconomic assumptions in the 1998 budget plan on Thursday but apparently put off a decision on total spending and revenue levels, divided over over how much to curb the deficit.
"The government determined three essential budgetary indices -- the planned growth of gross domestic product, inflation and wages," the government press office said in a statement.

As expected the budget would be constructed under assumptions that GDP will continue to grow at 5.5 percent annually and that inflation will fall to 9.5 percent year-on-year in December next year from 14.6 percent in May.
The statement said works on the budget were on track and that the finance minister was now preparing proposals for spending levels for particular ministries.

The brief statement provided no information on whether the cabinet made any decision on Finance Minister Marek Belka's crucial proposal to slash the budget gap to 1.9 percent of GDP next year from 2.8 percent planned for 1997.

Earlier this week the government spokeswoman Aleksandra Jakubowska said that on Thursday the cabinet would approve not only the budget's macroeconomic assumptions but also levels of spending, revenues and the deficit.
But on Wednesday, the Peasant Party (PSL) -- the smaller group in the government -- harshly criticised the finance ministry proposal to lower the deficit.
The daily Rzeczpospolita has reported Belka proposed to set the 1998 spending at 142.9 billion zlotys ($43.4 billion), revenues at 133.3 billion zlotys and deficit at 9.6 billion zlotys.

PSL obliged its cabinet members to vote against the proposal, saying it would hit farmers' income, curb investment and boost unemployment, even though the finance ministry had warned the budget gap must be radically lowered to stifle domestic demand and get the widening trade gap under control.

The central bank says that if the current account deficit, forecast to grow to $6 billion this year from $1.35 billion in 1996, expands too much in 1998 Poland might eventually have to devalue the zloty.
It says this would boost inflation and undermine economic growth.
But Peasant leader Waldemar Pawlak argued on Wednesday that curbing the demand would hit businesses, undermine exports' growth and consequently lower living standards.

The ex-communists, whose Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz has so far backed the finance ministry's plans for a tight 1998 budget, have dismissed PSL's objections as electioneering before the September parliamenary polls.
Belka's budgetary plans have also come under fire from the central bank, which said they do no go far enough.
The bank has suggested a balanced 1998 budget would be the best measure to avoid financial crisis recently experienced by the Czech Republic.
The Czech Republic had to devalue its currency and take strict anti-import measures, after its foreign trade deficit balooned and industrial output shrank.

The National Bank of Poland head Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz said in a newspaper on Thursday that a 1.9 percent deficit would make it more likely that an interest rate rise would be necessary to cool demand.
She added Poland could afford a 1.5 percent deficit next year if it led to a balanced budget in 1999.
